title: River Management & a Distinctive UK River
description: Causes of flooding, hard versus soft defences, and a named UK river landscape.
content_html:
Why Rivers Flood

A flood happens when the volume of water in a river exceeds the capacity of its channel. Both natural and human factors push rivers over the edge. Natural causes include heavy or prolonged rainfall, snowmelt on saturated ground, low-permeability rocks like clay that send water straight into the river, and steep upland slopes that speed runoff. Human causes include urbanisation (concrete prevents infiltration), deforestation (no roots to soak up water), and agriculture (compacted soil and field drains). All of these shorten lag time on the hydrograph — meaning the river peaks faster after a storm.

Key Fact

UK flooding is rarely one cause. Major events combine prolonged frontal rainfall, saturated catchments, urban runoff and historical changes to land use. Always discuss multiple causes in extended writing.

Hard Engineering: Containing the River

Hard engineering tries to contain or speed up the river. Dams and reservoirs store flood water and release it slowly, also providing drinking water and hydropower. The Kielder dam in Northumberland holds 200 million cubic metres of water but cost £167 million in the 1980s and drowned a Northumbrian valley. Channelisation — straightening and widening a river so flood water flows away faster — works for the protected stretch but pushes higher peaks downstream and damages river ecology by removing riffles, pools and bankside habitat. Even simple flood walls count as hard engineering: the Thames Barrier (1982) protects central London from tidal surge floods, and the Foss Barrier in York holds back surge water from the Ouse during winter floods.

Soft Engineering: Working With the Catchment

Soft engineering takes a different approach — it works with the catchment rather than fighting it. Floodplain zoning uses land-use planning instead of concrete: fields and parks beside the river are accepted as places where water will spread; housing and infrastructure are kept on higher ground. Washlands are deliberately maintained low areas next to the river that flood naturally, like the Ouse Washes in East Anglia where 24 km2 of farmland take up flood water in winter. River restoration removes old channelisation, allowing rivers to meander again. The River Skerne in Darlington was famously re-meandered in the 1990s; flood peaks downstream fell measurably and wildlife returned. Combined with upland peat rewetting in the Pennines and tree planting in upper catchments, soft engineering is increasingly the preferred long-term strategy.

A Distinctive UK River: The River Tees

The River Tees flows 137 km from Cross Fell in the North Pennines to the North Sea at Middlesbrough. Its journey runs through every classic landform. In the upper course at High Force, the river drops 22 metres over a layer of hard whinstone capping softer carboniferous limestone, retreating slowly upstream and leaving a steep wooded gorge. The middle course swings through a wide-floored valley with classic meanders near Yarm. The lower course flows across a broad floodplain to a large tidal estuary at Teesside.

Human activity has reshaped the Tees throughout its course. Cow Green Reservoir (built 1970) regulates flow upstream. Channel improvements at Yarm and a flood-relief storage area at Hurworth Burn protect riverside towns. The estuary has been heavily industrialised since the 1850s — reclaimed for steelworks, chemical plants and the modern port — reducing the natural mudflats and salt marsh that once buffered storm surges.

Storm Arwen in November 2021 and Storm Babet in October 2023 brought serious flooding to towns along the Tees including Yarm and Stockton. Even with reservoirs and channelisation, the lower Tees catchment is small relative to the rainfall it can receive in a single weather system. Saturated ground from earlier rainfall reduces infiltration; tidal locking at the estuary — where high tide blocks river outflow — can amplify upstream peaks. Defences are protection, not prevention.

A warmer atmosphere holds about 7% more water vapour for every 1°C of warming, so heavier rainfall events are becoming more common in the UK. The Met Office has linked record-breaking 2015 (Cumbria) and 2019–20 (Yorkshire, South Wales) floods to climate change. Future-proofing rivers therefore requires both grey infrastructure (defences) and green infrastructure (rewetted upland peat, replanted catchments, washlands) so the catchment as a whole holds more water before it reaches the channel.

Key Fact

The River Tees rises at Cross Fell (~893 m), flows 137 km through the High Force waterfall, meanders near Yarm, and enters the North Sea at Middlesbrough. Each course has been shaped by both physical and human change.
exam_tip_html: Edexcel rewards specific named places and figures on river-management questions. For 8-mark answers, balance one hard engineering example (Kielder dam, Cow Green) with one soft engineering example (Skerne re-meandering, Ouse Washes), give a cost or benefit number, and conclude with which would best suit the river you studied. Avoid generic answers about ‘sandbags’ — markers want named UK schemes.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK flooding is a mix of natural (rainfall, geology, slope) and human (urbanisation, deforestation, drainage) causes.
  • Hard engineering (dams, channelisation) protects but moves the problem; soft engineering (zoning, washlands, restoration) reduces peaks naturally.
  • The River Tees illustrates every river course and the trade-offs of human management.

Large engineered structures used to control river flow, such as dams, channelisation and flood walls.

practice_questions.text: Which is an example of soft engineering for river management?
practice_questions.marks: A. Channelisation  |  B. Sea wall  |  C. Floodplain zoning (correct)  |  D. Dam — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: State two human causes of river flooding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clearly stated causes (e.g. urbanisation increasing surface runoff; deforestation reducing interception). Secure: Two valid causes briefly stated. Developing: One cause. Emerging: Vague mention of human activity.

practice_questions.text: Explain how urbanisation increases the risk of river flooding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Concrete and tarmac are impermeable; rainwater cannot infiltrate; drains carry it directly into rivers; lag time falls and peak discharge rises. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: Mentions concrete without consequence. Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and main features of one named UK river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a river (e.g. Tees), states source and mouth, gives a length, names two named features along the course (waterfall, meander, estuary). Secure: Three of the above. Developing: Names a river only. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why some UK river catchments flood more often than others.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed contrasts: rock type (impermeable clay vs porous chalk), slope (upland steep vs lowland flat), land use (urban vs forested), with named examples. Secure: Two contrasts with examples. Developing: Lists factors without contrast. Emerging: One reason only.

practice_questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of using hard and soft engineering together to manage flood risk on a named UK river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing hard schemes (dam, channelisation) and soft schemes (washlands, restoration) for a clearly named river, with figures, advantages and limitations, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both approaches with examples. Developing: Description-led. Emerging: One approach only.

title: Glaciated Upland Landscapes & Management
description: Erosional and depositional landforms of UK glaciated uplands, and pressures on them today.
content_html:
Why Glaciated Uplands Look the Way They Do

Around 18,000 years ago much of upland Britain lay under thick ice. Glaciers shaped the rock as they flowed, leaving today’s dramatic peaks, valleys and lakes. The UK’s glaciated uplands — the Lake District, Snowdonia, the Cairngorms, the Scottish Highlands — are relict landscapes: the ice itself has gone, but the landforms remain. Today’s climate continues to chip at them through freeze-thaw weathering and slope processes, but the dramatic shapes are inheritances from the last Ice Age.

How Glaciers Erode

Glaciers erode in two main ways. Plucking happens when meltwater at the base of the ice freezes around loose rock; as the glacier moves on, the rock is ripped out of the bedrock. Abrasion happens when the rocks frozen into the glacier’s base scrape across the bedrock below, leaving long parallel scratches called striations. The two processes work together: plucking takes blocks out, abrasion smooths what is left.

Key Fact

The four key erosional landforms are corries (armchair-shaped hollows), arêtes (knife-edge ridges), pyramidal peaks and U-shaped glacial troughs. They form when ice plucks and abrades hard upland rock.

Erosional Landforms

A corrie (also called a cwm in Wales or cirque in the Alps) is an armchair-shaped hollow on a mountain side. Snow accumulated in a sheltered hollow and compressed into ice; rotational movement of that ice plucked the back wall and abraded the floor; meltwater froze into cracks and prised out more rock. After the ice melted, a small lake (a tarn) often formed in the hollow. Red Tarn below Helvellyn is a textbook example. Where two corries developed back-to-back on opposite sides of a ridge, the rock between them was eroded down to a knife-edge arête — Striding Edge in the Lake District is a famous one. Where three or more corries surrounded a peak, the result is a pyramidal peak like Snowdon or the Matterhorn.

When a glacier flowed downhill it widened, deepened and straightened the valley it occupied. River-cut V-shaped valleys became U-shaped glacial troughs with steep sides and flat floors. The original interlocking spurs of the river were sheared off into truncated spurs. Tributary glaciers cut their valleys less deeply; once the ice melted, those valleys hung above the main trough as hanging valleys, often with a waterfall plunging from the rim. Llyn Idwal in Snowdonia and Wast Water in the Lake District sit in classic glacial troughs.

Depositional Landforms

Glaciers also dump material when they melt. Unsorted rocks and clay carried by ice are called moraine. Ground moraine blankets valley floors. Terminal moraine piles up at the snout of a glacier where ice melts as fast as it advances; it forms a curved ridge across the valley. Smaller landforms include drumlins — egg-shaped hills of moraine, with the steep end pointing in the direction the ice came from — and crag and tail, where harder rock protected softer rock from erosion behind it (Edinburgh Castle Rock and the Royal Mile is the classic example).

Sheep farming dominates UK uplands — hardy breeds like Herdwick graze where almost nothing else can. Conifer forestry plantations occupy steeper slopes, especially in the Lake District and Northumberland. Settlement sits in the valleys: stone-built villages like Grasmere and Beddgelert serve walkers and tourists. Reservoirs drown some valleys to supply distant cities — Thirlmere in the Lake District has fed Manchester since 1894. Each use changes the landscape, sometimes preserving its character (drystone walls, hedgerows), sometimes degrading it (overgrazing, soil erosion).

A Distinctive UK Glaciated Upland: The Lake District

The Lake District National Park covers 2,362 km2 in north-west England. Its slate, granite and volcanic rocks were folded by the Caledonian orogeny then sculpted by Ice Age glaciers into an iconic landscape: 16 main lakes filling glacial troughs, arêtes like Striding Edge and Sharp Edge, and pyramidal peaks like Helvellyn (950 m). Today over 18 million visitors a year bring £1.4 billion to the local economy but also create challenges: footpath erosion on Helvellyn cost the National Trust around £1.5 million to repair in the 2010s; second-home ownership pushes house prices beyond local wages; lake water quality has fallen as tourism intensifies.

Reservoirs supply clean water at scale and provide hydropower, but they drown valleys (and sometimes villages, as at Mardale Green under Haweswater). Wind farms generate renewable energy but change visual character — a major issue in protected upland landscapes. Tourism funds conservation and rural businesses but pressures footpaths, wildlife and housing. Conservation through National Park status protects landscapes but adds planning costs for residents who want to extend their homes. There is no neutral choice in upland development — every option carries trade-offs.

Key Fact

The Lake District contains pyramidal peaks (Helvellyn), arêtes (Striding Edge), corries with tarns (Red Tarn), glacial troughs (Wast Water) and ribbon lakes — all carved by ice 18,000 years ago and now under tourism pressure.
exam_tip_html: Edexcel often pairs a photo of a glacial landform with a question asking you to identify and explain. Always name the landform AND the process that made it. For 6-mark and 8-mark questions on land use, name two specific land uses (sheep farming, forestry, reservoirs, tourism) and give an advantage and a disadvantage of each. Conclude with a judgement on which use the landscape can sustain best.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Glacial uplands are relict landscapes — the ice has gone, but its erosional and depositional landforms remain.
  • Plucking and abrasion produce corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, glacial troughs, hanging valleys and truncated spurs.
  • UK uplands face competing pressures from farming, forestry, reservoirs, conservation and tourism — the Lake District shows all five.

glossary_terms.definition: A landscape that was once shaped by glaciers but no longer has active ice.
The breakdown of rock by repeated freezing and thawing of water in cracks.
Glacial erosion in which meltwater freezes around loose rocks at the base of the ice and tears them out as the glacier moves on.

practice_questions.text: Which landform is an armchair-shaped hollow on a mountain side?
practice_questions.marks: A. Drumlin  |  B. Corrie (correct)  |  C. Arête  |  D. Truncated spur — 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Define plucking as a glacial erosion process.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Meltwater at the base of a glacier freezes around loose rocks; as the ice moves it tears the rocks out of the bedrock. Secure: Ice freezes around rocks and pulls them out. Developing: Ice picks up rocks. Emerging: Vague reference to glaciation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a pyramidal peak is formed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more corries develop on different sides of a mountain; their back walls retreat into the mountain by plucking and abrasion; eventually they leave a sharp pyramid-shaped peak. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: Names corries without process. Emerging: Names the landform only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and main features of one glaciated upland landscape in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the Lake District, places it NW England, gives area or named lake/peak, plus a glacial landform such as Striding Edge or Wast Water. Secure: Three of these. Developing: Names the landscape only. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity has affected a glaciated upland landscape you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed impacts (e.g. sheep farming preventing tree regrowth; reservoirs drowning valleys; tourism causing footpath erosion) with named places and figures. Secure: Two impacts with examples. Developing: Lists impacts. Emerging: One impact only.

practice_questions.text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of developing UK glaciated uplands for tourism, water supply or renewable energy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing economic and environmental advantages against disadvantages for at least two named uses, with developed examples and a justified conclusion that links to a named landscape. Secure: Both sides covered with examples. Developing: Description-led, partial weighing. Emerging: One use only.
